stufen.name: Rude
stufen.satz: Have you got a bloody minute or not?

gruppen.titel: Short forms: how people really speak
gruppen.intro: In fast speech, sounds disappear. Don't write these forms in a letter or an exam – but you will hear them every day.

eintraege.std: going to, want to, have got to

eintraege.bsp: I'm staying in cos it's raining.
Are you coming? – Nope, I'm too tired.

eintraege.std: kind of, sort of (= a bit)

eintraege.info: Very common in songs and in some accents, but it counts as non-standard. Never write it in an exam.

gruppen.intro: These words are relaxed, but not rude. With friends and colleagues they are normal. In a formal letter or at an office, use the word on the right.

eintraege.info: In the UK, cheers means thanks or bye, not only what you say with a drink.

eintraege.std: friend; a friendly way to talk to someone

eintraege.bsp: Do you fancy a cup of tea?
Don't worry, we've got loads of time.
Let's sit down and have a cuppa.
Their kids are at school until three.
Put your stuff in the car.
Let's grab a sandwich before the train.

eintraege.info: In England this is often just a greeting. A short answer is enough.

eintraege.bsp: We went to a very posh restaurant.

gruppen.intro: In class you learn the normal numbers. You will still hear these forms a lot – you need to understand them, but you don't have to say them.

eintraege.info: No -s in the plural: ten quid, not ten quids.

eintraege.bsp: Can you lend me a tenner?

eintraege.info: Say it like the letter: ten p.
Not a mistake: in phone numbers most British people say oh, not zero. 77 is often double seven.

eintraege.bsp: I'll be there in a couple of minutes.

gruppen.intro: Slang changes fast. Young people use it with each other. An adult who uses it at the office often sounds strange.

eintraege.std: isn't it? (at the end of a sentence)
eintraege.info: Typical of London and young people. Never in a work email.
Here it does not mean ill – the opposite!

eintraege.bsp: At the weekend I just chill at home.
I'm gutted we lost the match.
I can't come out tonight, I'm skint.
He's still salty about losing the game.
Best pizza in town, no cap.
eintraege.info: From American slang. Young people use it; older people often don't know it.

gruppen.intro: You should understand these words – in films, on the street, at a football match. Saying them yourself is risky: you can sound aggressive very quickly.

eintraege.info: Mild. Fine with friends, not in a formal meeting.
Very British. Mild today, but not for a job interview.
Not a swear word, just very direct.

eintraege.bsp: Shut up, I'm trying to watch the film!
eintraege.info: Among friends it can also mean ‘No way!’: Shut up! You got the job?
Very common, but rude. Not in front of your boss, at an office or near children.

eintraege.bsp: He was pissed after five pints.
eintraege.info: A British and an American speaker can mean different things. Pissed off means angry in both.

eintraege.bsp: Some idiot has parked in front of my garage!
eintraege.info: If you say it to someone's face, it is an insult.
You will hear it in films and on the street. Never use it at work, with strangers or with the police.

hoeflich.zu: Could you be a bit quieter, please?
I don't really feel like it.
Could you give me a moment, please?

recht: Swearing is not a crime in itself in the UK. But threatening or abusive words that cause someone harassment, alarm or distress can be an offence under the Public Order Act 1986. At work, swearing at a colleague or a customer can lead to a warning or even losing your job.
